opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think sparsity is one of the most promising directions right now, and the basic reason is economics. With a mixture-of-experts model, you decouple the total number of parameters, which roughly tracks how much knowledge and capacity the model has, from the compute you spend per token. You can have a model with hundreds of billions or even a trillion parameters, but each token only activates a small fraction of them. So you get much of the quality of a very large model at the training and inference cost of a much smaller one.

What's been interesting over the last year or two is that the field keeps pushing toward more sparsity: more experts, smaller experts, and a lower ratio of active to total parameters. Early MoE models might route to two out of eight experts. Now you see configurations with hundreds of fine-grained experts, where only a handful fire per token. Empirically, that keeps working. The scaling behavior holds up, and you get better quality for the same FLOPs.

From my perspective, coming from the systems and hardware side, this is exciting and also a challenge. Sparse models are harder to run efficiently. You're doing a lot of small matrix multiplies instead of a few big ones, and you have routing, load balancing, and communication across GPUs when experts live on different devices. Memory bandwidth becomes a big deal, especially at inference, because you still have to store and move all those parameters even if you only use some of them per token. So there's a lot of room for better kernels, better parallelism strategies, and co-designing the architecture with the hardware so that sparsity actually turns into wall-clock speedups and not just theoretical FLOP savings.

More broadly, I think it reflects a shift in how we think about scaling. Instead of just making everything denser and bigger, we're asking where we actually need compute. Not every token needs the full model. Sparsity is one way to allocate compute more intelligently, and I expect we'll see more of that, both in MoE and in other forms of conditional computation.

r001.rationale: The response says increasing MoE sparsity yields better quality for the same FLOPs, by activating only a small fraction of a much larger model’s parameters per token.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that gets me excited is that sparse MoE is basically the clearest example we have of decoupling the number of parameters from the amount of compute you spend per token. For a long time those two things were tied together. If you wanted a smarter model, you made it bigger, and making it bigger meant every single token had to flow through every single weight. MoE breaks that. You can have a model with a huge amount of knowledge stored in the parameters, but each token only touches a small fraction of them.

And what we've seen over the last couple of years is that the sparsity ratio keeps going up. Early MoEs were maybe eight experts, pick two. Now you see things like 128 or 256 experts and you're activating a handful of them, so you're at active parameter ratios of a few percent. And the surprising part is that it keeps working. The quality per unit of compute keeps improving as you push sparsity, and it's not obvious a priori that it should.

From where I sit, which is a lot about hardware and systems, this is interesting because it changes what the bottleneck is. Dense models are mostly about matmul FLOPs, and we've gotten very good at that. Sparse MoE shifts the problem toward memory capacity, memory bandwidth, and communication, because you have to hold all those experts somewhere and route tokens to them. Those are harder problems, honestly, and they're more interesting problems. It means the next few years of systems work isn't just making the GEMM faster. It's about how you lay out experts across devices, how you do all-to-all efficiently, how you batch at inference when different tokens want different experts, how you deal with load imbalance.

There's also an inference angle that I think is underappreciated. For a lot of deployments, you're memory bandwidth bound during decoding. You're reading weights for every token you generate. With a sparse model, the weights you actually read per token is small, so in principle you can get a lot of model quality at a decode cost closer to a much smaller dense model. That's a really nice trade if you can get the systems right.

And then the last thing is that it feels like we've only explored a small corner of the design space. Expert granularity, shared experts, how many experts per token, whether experts should be in attention too, how routing interacts with long context. All of that is still pretty open. So it's exciting both because it clearly works and because there's a lot of room left.

r001.rationale: The response says increasing sparsity lets MoE models improve quality per unit of compute, while each token uses only a small fraction of the parameters.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that you can increase the model’s capacity without increasing the computation per token by the same amount. You have a large collection of experts, but each token only uses a small subset. That gives you another way to scale: more parameters to learn from the data, while keeping the active computation relatively small.

The interesting challenge is turning that theoretical efficiency into actual speed. If each expert gets only a few tokens, the matrix multiplications become small, and moving tokens between GPUs can become expensive. So fewer FLOPs doesn’t automatically mean lower latency.

That’s why I find this direction exciting: the architecture and the systems really have to evolve together. If we can make routing, communication, and computation work well together, increasingly sparse models could give us substantially more capability for the same compute budget.

r001.rationale: It says increasingly sparse models could provide substantially more capability for the same compute budget, explaining that more experts increase capacity while each token uses only a small subset.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that you can grow the model’s capacity without increasing the computation for every token by the same amount. You might have a large number of experts, but only activate a few of them for each token. So you can have more parameters available while keeping the active computation relatively small.

The interesting challenge is making that sparsity translate into actual speed. Routing tokens, moving data between GPUs, and balancing work across experts all have costs. If each expert gets only a tiny amount of work, the hardware can become inefficient. So it’s a really interesting intersection of architecture and systems: how do we design the model and the implementation together so that fewer theoretical FLOPs actually means faster training and inference?

r001.rationale: The response says sparsity allows more parameters while keeping active computation relatively small, but it does not connect that tradeoff to obtaining greater intelligence for the same compute budget.
